# Welcome to the era of embodied AI: Introducing AA-Robotics v0.1

We are launching AA-Robotics v0.1, our research preview that measures frontier language model performance on understanding, planning, and acting in the physical world. In v0.1, each model is given control of a 6-axis robot arm (5 joints and a gripper) and a simple objective. We’re releasing results for our first eight tasks today.

## Introducing AA-Robotics v0.1

Since the beginning of 2026, frontier language models have made enormous progress in their ability to control robot arms. We now believe that the future of robotics is likely to involve strong generalist agents, and conclude that tracking progress of language models for robotics tasks is going to be important - even if frontier language models are unsuitable for production robotics use on their own.

AA-Robotics v0.1 is our research preview of the simplest experiment we have designed to test this - language models in coding agent harnesses directly controlling a robot arm. Each model is given control of a 6-axis robot arm (5 joints and a gripper) and a simple objective for each task.

We find that frontier language models in coding agent harnesses have indeed recently become capable of directly manipulating robot arms for simple tasks. Today, they are far too slow and expensive for any kind of production usage - nearly two orders of magnitude worse than human baselines. We expect this to change quickly.

GPT-6 Astra places first in AA-Robotics v0.1 with a score of 69, followed by GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1. GPT-6 Astra took 30 minutes and cost $16.36 on average per task.

### AA-Robotics Score

Each attempt is scored out of 100: completing the task scores 100, and a partial result earns points for the progress made.

## The eight tasks

AA-Robotics v0.1 initially includes eight tabletop tasks, modeled on everyday activities, to evaluate a range of robotics capabilities: control and dexterity, such as precise grasping and handling objects, spatial reasoning, such as understanding how objects interact with one another, and adaptability, measuring how models respond to the unexpected.

## How AA-Robotics works

Models run in an isolated container with brief instructions: how to reach the robot arm (via a simple HTTP API), which arm it is (a Hiwonder NexArm, with no further specifications), and how to submit an attempt as complete. They can view the scene through four cameras, three mounted around the table and one on the arm’s wrist, and can write and run code in the container to plan and send movements.

Once a model has submitted a task for review, the end state is graded against the task’s pass criteria. A pass scores 100, with points awarded for partial success in the case of an incomplete task. All task attempts are zero-shot.

## Time & cost

Today’s language models are roughly 100 times slower than a human on AA-Robotics v0.1, taking about half an hour per task compared with a human average of 20 seconds. In aggregate, four of the five models tested look similar, at about 30 minutes per task, while Gemini 4 Argon is the slowest at 52 minutes. However, these averages hide large differences between tasks.

GPT-6 Astra pressed the red button in 2.2 minutes, whereas Claude Fable 5.1 spent about ten minutes understanding and planning before its first action. The largest difference came on the crocodile placement task, where GPT-6.1 Sol declared itself complete after five minutes, compared with 45 for Claude Opus 5.5, a ninefold difference. Across all tasks, Gemini 4 Argon was the slowest to act, spending an average of 21 minutes observing and reasoning before its first action, nearly twice as long as any other model.

### Time per Task

### AA-Robotics Score vs. Time per Task

The gap between humans and models is narrower on cost: the most cost-effective model costs about ten times as much as a person paid the average US hourly wage, against nearly 100 times as long on time. Between models, GPT-6.1 Sol is the cheapest, at $1.93 per task on average, while GPT-6 Astra, the most expensive, costs $16.36, more than eight times as much as Sol, for a score only four points higher (69 against 65). Given the novelty of the arm and scene, and the large volume of visual information the models must process, most of the cost lands on input: 70% of the spend goes on context.

## How each model spent its time

As expected, models spend a large portion of the initial task time calibrating the arm and understanding the scene, continuing this up until taking the first action. After this point, the majority of time is spent planning movement, with relatively short, precise arm movements between each longer planning step. Camera views and note writing are relatively small fractions of the overall time.

Interestingly, models often continue to refine their attempts long after reaching a passing state. GPT-6.1 Sol, for example, builds a passing tower after ~17 minutes, only to subsequently fail the task. It remains to be seen how models will improve their ability to reason about task completion in physical space.

## Physical accuracy

Grasping and fine manipulation were key skills to test in AA-Robotics v0.1, as they point the way not only to more precise control tasks, but more importantly to tool use and the far wider range of capabilities it unlocks.

GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 performed best with the highest proportion of successful attempts (~45%), indicating a degree of close control, whilst GPT-6.1 Sol, scored worst, at 28%. Gemini 4 Argon fell in between at 36%, with many of its misses closing just above or beside the block it was reaching for.

### Outcome of Every Grasp Attempt

- Successful Grasp

- Missed, Partial, or Wrong-Object Grasp

Grasps were attempted in the Place Crocodile, Pour Drink, Tidy Box, Match Shapes, Build Tower, and Measure Box tasks. Successful is defined as holding the intended object through its lift or carry, and missed, partial, or wrong-object where the gripper did not close on the object, closed on it before it slipped, dropped, or could not be lifted, or took a different object by mistake.

# Gemini 4 Argon: Google is back as one of the top three labs in intelligence achieved

Google’s new Gemini 4 Argon equals GPT-6 Astra on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 60% of the Cost per Task with discounted prices

Gemini 4 Argon is Google DeepMind’s first proprietary model above the Flash class in over 7 months. With high reasoning (the highest available), it scores 53 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, matching GPT-6 Astra (max, 53) and 1 point ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 52), with gains driven by lower hallucinations and stronger agentic capabilities.

At its current 50% pricing discount and with cache discounts increased to 95%, Gemini 4 Argon costs $1.99 per Intelligence Index task, 60% of GPT-6 Astra (max), but 2.7x GPT-6.1 Sol (max). After the discount ends, this will rise to $3.98 (~1.2x GPT-6 Astra (max)).

Gemini 4 Argon is currently being rolled out to selected users and is not publicly available. The 50% discount is an initial promotion. Google has not yet confirmed the promotion end date

Key benchmarking results for Gemini 4 Argon with high reasoning:

➤ Google returns as one of the top three labs on intelligence: Gemini 4 Argon (high) scores 53 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, matching GPT-6 Astra (max, 53) and 1 point ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 52). This is 23 points above Google’s previous non-Flash model, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (30) and 12 points ahead of Gemini 3.8 Flash (high)

➤ Launch discounts of 50% make Gemini 4 Argon competitive on Cost per Task: At current discounted pricing, Gemini 4 Argon (high) costs $1.99 per Intelligence Index task, 60% of GPT-6 Astra (max, $3.26) for a comparable level of intelligence. This cost efficiency is driven by lower token prices, rather than reduced token use, with Gemini 4 Argon averaging 62k output tokens per task, compared with 27k for GPT-6 Astra (max). Google has not yet confirmed the promotion end date, but on standard pricing, Cost per Task will increase to $3.98

➤ Stronger agentic performance: Historically a weaker area for Gemini models, Gemini 4 Argon shows improvements across agentic evaluations. It ranks #1 on AutomationBench-AA at 78%, 7 points ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max, 71%). On Terminal Bench 4, Gemini 4 Argon achieves 57%, a + 53 point improvement from Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, only behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max, 64%), Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 60%) and GPT-6 Astra (59%). On AA-Briefcase, it reaches 1494 Elo. This is driven by a 65% rubric pass rate, the highest we have recorded, but lower Analytical Quality (1576 Elo) and Presentation Quality (1308 Elo)

➤ Lowest hallucination rate among leading models: On AA-Omniscience, Gemini 4 Argon has a 15% hallucination rate, the lowest of any model scoring 45+ on the Intelligence Index, compared with 51% for GPT-6 Astra (max) and 54% for GPT-6.1 Sol (max). This means Argon is much more likely to acknowledge when it does not know an answer rather than guess incorrectly. On accuracy, Gemini 4 Argon scores 50%, a 5 point decrease from Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, and 13 points below GPT-6 Astra (max, 63%). With this slightly lower accuracy, its overall AA-Omniscience score of 42 remains in line with GPT-6 Astra (43) and GPT-6.1 Sol (42)

Key model details:

➤ Context Window: 1M tokens

➤ Multimodality: Text, image, video, and speech input, with text output

➤ Pricing: $4/$20 per 1M input/output tokens at standard pricing, currently discounted 50% to $2/$10 for at least one month. Cached input tokens receive a 95% discount ($0.10 per 1M at discounted pricing), up from 90% on Gemini 3.8 Flash

➤ Long Decode Continuation: We tested Gemini 4 Argon with Long Decode Continuation, a new Gemini API feature that pauses long responses and resumes them across follow-up calls. This lets reasoning run up to 1M output tokens without request timeouts

For further analysis, see https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/gemini-4-argon
